editorialCommentary.finding: The later editor identifies Peripatetic and Illuminationist positions, cites the proofs and objections in Ṣadrā, Ibn Sīnā and Bahmanyār, and explicates the examples. These attributions are not added authorial sentences.

At182n3, the editor says efficient cause here does not mean a separate bestower of existence and quotes a pupil interpreting the priority as causal, not temporal. At183n1 he cross-refers to his earlier disagreement on matter/form priority.

explanation: All21 Arabic and17 English paragraphs are accounted for. Both proofs, both first-proof objections, the individual-form objection, the complete conclusion, and both stated consequences are present.

The conclusion distinguishes the dependence of secondary matter on specific form from corporeal form’s partnership in preserving prime matter. The English preserves causal priority and the replacement of corporeality with specific form; it does not assert temporal priority.
The first objection’s singular question can refer to بناء. A dual correction is not automatically obligatory merely because the later editor prints one.
No original authorial footnote or quotation locator was omitted from this chapter. Later references to Suhrawardī, Ṣadrā, Ibn Sīnā and Bahmanyār are editor apparatus.

new.text: The 1428 editor at vol.1 p.186 n.2 objects to the author’s middle-segment example. He prefers Sabzawārī’s examples of a point between parts of a line, a line between parts of a surface, a surface between parts of a body, and an instant between parts of time. He argues that a middle piece does not distinguish continuous from discrete quantity, since a middle unit could similarly be selected in seven. Both editions retain the author’s example in the body; this is an attributed philosophical objection, not an attested replacement.

new.text: At 1428 vol.1 p.188 n.2, the editor quotes a pupil of the author who disputes the final claim about irregular figures. The objection is that an irregular figure may be one actual shape; imagining its partition for calculation does not establish actual composition, any more than imagining two triangles makes a square actually composite. Both editions retain the author’s conclusion. This note reports the objection without silently substituting it for the source text.
